meta.axis: geology of other solvents/temperatures + silica- and life-built rock
meta.note: T_K values are representative surface/means: Titan 94, Venus 737 surface, Enceladus ~75 surface, Europa ~102, Triton 38, Mars ~210 mean, 55 Cnc e ~2700 dayside max.

worlds.name: Titan
landforms: methane-ethane seas and lakes (north polar)
dendritic river channels and rounded water-ice cobbles (Huygens site)
linear (longitudinal) organic dunes ~100 m high, equatorial
labyrinth terrain: dissected organic plateaus with deep valleys
karst-like sharp-edged lake depressions (dissolution)
candidate cryovolcanic mountains/flows (disputed)
drivers: UV/charged-particle photolysis of CH4+N2 makes tholin haze that settles as organic sediment
methane rain and runoff erode water-ice bedrock
winds pile organic sand into longitudinal dunes
dissolution of organics in liquid hydrocarbons (karst analogue), slow (geological time)
seasonal methane cycle (Titan year ~29.5 Earth yr)

control_map.Light: Bright => tholin orange stain; Dim => little tholin, pale frost field (eco-04 vs eco-05)
control_map.Time: karst depth, dune field extent, labyrinth dissection
control_map.Recipe: bedrock is water ice + organics, not silicate; Si-heavy recipe = our game invention

worlds.name: Venus
worlds.solvent: concentrated sulfuric acid in cloud deck ~48-70 km; surface is dry supercritical CO2
landforms: tesserae: highly folded/faulted highland plateaus (possibly felsic, silica-richer)
pancake (steep-sided) domes, mean ~24 km wide, ~700 m high
coronae: ring-shaped volcano-tectonic uplifts
vast lava plains and lava channels
radar-bright 'snow' (metal frost) on highlands above ~2.5-4.5 km
drivers: mantle plumes and viscous lava (domes, coronae)
crustal deformation (tesserae)
gas-solid chemical weathering by CO2/SO2 at 737 K
volatile metal compounds condense in cooler highlands (Pb/Bi sulfides proposed)
colours: pale yellow-white sulfuric-acid cloud tops (unknown UV absorber)

control_map.Sea: Acid (the cloud layer, not the surface)
control_map.Heat: Warm in cloud deck (~300-350 K at 50-55 km); surface is Hot extreme
control_map.Light: bright diffuse, no shadows under clouds

worlds.caveat: No liquid acid sea exists on Venus' surface; our Acid sea is a game abstraction of the cloud deck [INFERRED].

worlds.name: Enceladus
worlds.solvent: liquid water ocean (salty, alkaline) under ice
landforms: 'tiger stripe' fractures at south pole
water-vapour/ice-grain plumes and jets
resurfaced, crater-poor south polar terrain
drivers: tidal heating
hydrothermal water-rock reaction >90 °C at seafloor (silica nanoparticles in E-ring grains)
H2 in plume consistent with serpentinization
colours: brilliant white ice (highest albedo in solar system)
blue-green tint along stripes in enhanced colour

control_map.Recipe: Si+O: silica nanoparticles are direct evidence of silica-saturated hot water

sources.cite: Porco et al. 2006, Cassini observes the active south pole of Enceladus, Science

worlds.name: Europa
worlds.solvent: liquid water ocean under ice shell
landforms: chaos terrain: rafts of broken ice in a jumbled matrix
double ridges and lineae
drivers: melt lenses of liquid water in the shallow shell collapse the surface
tidal flexing

sources.cite: Schmidt et al. 2011, Active formation of chaos terrain over shallow subsurface water on Europa, Nature

worlds.name: Icy moons: ammonia-water cryovolcanism (general; Triton)
worlds.solvent: ammonia-water melt (eutectic ~176 K); Triton geysers of N2 gas
landforms: viscous ammonia-water cryolava flows/domes (theorised)
Triton geyser plumes ~8 km tall with dark wind streaks
drivers: ammonia lowers water's melting point by ~100 K
solar-heated subsurface N2 ice venting (Triton)
worlds.caveat: Violet/plum ammonia palette is [game], not observed.

sources.cite: Kargel 1992, Ammonia-water volcanism on icy satellites: phase relations at 1 atmosphere, Icarus
Soderblom et al. 1990, Triton's geyser-like plumes, Science

worlds.name: Mars
worlds.solvent: none today (ancient liquid water); thin CO2 air
landforms: iron-oxide dust and dune fields
layered sedimentary deposits (Valles Marineris, crater fills)
opaline-silica nodules and digitate 'cauliflower' structures (Home Plate, Gusev)
recurring slope lineae (seasonal dark streaks)
drivers: ancient water-deposited sediments
oxidation of iron (hematite, nanophase Fe oxides)
volcanic hydrothermal silica (hot spring or fumarole)
RSL now mostly explained as dry granular flows (disputed water role)

control_map.Heat: Hot dial gives our red-canyon look, real Mars is cold
control_map.Time: Very old: red stain + layered canyon walls (eco-01, eco-10)

worlds.name: Lava worlds (55 Cancri e, CoRoT-7b)
landforms: dayside magma lakes/ocean (inferred)
volcanic outgassing atmosphere (CO/CO2 on 55 Cnc e)
by Earth analogy: lava tubes, skylights, obsidian glass, vesicular pumice
drivers: tidal locking, extreme stellar irradiation
dayside ~2700 K vs nightside ~1400 K (55 Cnc e)
rapid quenching makes glass

control_map.Recipe: Si+O = silicate melt; most literal 'silicon world'

silica_biogenic.name: Hot-spring siliceous sinter & geyserite terraces
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Silica-saturated geothermal water cools and evaporates, precipitating opal-A; microbial mats template and trap it
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: up to ~2.5 kg/m²/yr at El Tatio (in situ); mm-scale per year typical
colours: orange, yellow, green microbial mats banded by temperature

sources.cite: Campbell et al. 2015, Geyserite in hot-spring siliceous sinter, Earth-Sci. Rev.
Nicolau et al. 2014, Physico-chemical and environmental controls on siliceous sinter formation at El Tatio, J. Volcanol. Geotherm. Res.
Ruff & Farmer 2016, Silica deposits on Mars with features resembling hot spring biosignatures at El Tatio, Nat. Commun.

silica_biogenic.name: Opal (precious)
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Ordered packing of uniform silica spheres (~150-350 nm) settled from silica gel; diffraction gives play of colour
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: slow; formation timescale debated (thousands to millions of years)

sources.cite: Sanders 1964, Colour of precious opal, Nature

silica_biogenic.name: Chert and jasper
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Diagenetic recrystallisation of biogenic or chemical silica into microcrystalline quartz

sources.cite: Konhauser et al. 2017, Iron formations: a global record of Neoarchaean to Palaeoproterozoic environmental history, Earth-Sci. Rev.
Allwood et al. 2006, Stromatolite reef from the Early Archaean era of Australia, Nature

silica_biogenic.name: Banded iron formations (BIF)
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Alternating layers of iron oxides and chert precipitated from Fe-rich, silica-saturated Archaean-Paleoproterozoic seawater as O2 rose; microbial role debated

sources.cite: Konhauser et al. 2017, Iron formations: a global record of Neoarchaean to Palaeoproterozoic environmental history, Earth-Sci. Rev.

silica_biogenic.name: Diatomite / radiolarian ooze -> radiolarite
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Plankton build opal shells (frustules, lattice skeletons); shells rain to seafloor as ooze, later lithify to diatomite or radiolarite/chert
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: ooze accumulates ~mm to cm per kyr; gross biogenic silica production ~240 Tmol Si/yr

sources.cite: Tréguer & De La Rocha 2013, The world ocean silica cycle, Annu. Rev. Mar. Sci.

silica_biogenic.name: Glass-sponge (hexactinellid) reefs
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Sponges build fused opal-silica skeletal lattices; new sponges settle on dead skeletons, which trap sediment
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: individual sponges ~cm/yr [POP, not verified]; reefs ~9,000 yr old, up to ~20 m high [POP]
examples: Hecate Strait and Strait of Georgia (British Columbia)

sources.cite: Krautter et al. 2001, Discovery of a 'living dinosaur': modern hexactinellid sponge reefs off British Columbia, Facies
Maldonado et al. 1999, Decline in Mesozoic reef-building sponges explained by silicon limitation, Nature

silica_biogenic.name: Stromatolites & microbialites
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Microbial mats trap/bind sediment and precipitate carbonate (micrite) layer by layer
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: ~0.3-0.5 mm/yr at Shark Bay [POP, not verified here]
silica_biogenic.status: consensus (carbonate; silicified examples common in Archaean chert)

sources.cite: Suosaari et al. 2016, New multi-scale perspectives on the stromatolites of Shark Bay, Sci. Rep.
Reid et al. 2000, The role of microbes in accretion, lamination and early lithification of modern marine stromatolites, Nature
Allwood et al. 2006, Stromatolite reef from the Early Archaean era of Australia, Nature

silica_biogenic.name: Chemical (silicate) gardens
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Metal-salt seed dissolves in alkali silicate; a semipermeable silicate membrane forms, osmotic pressure ruptures it and a jet precipitates new hollow tube
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: seconds to minutes; mm/s to cm/min
colours: take the metal's colour: blue (Cu), orange-brown (Fe), green (Ni), white (Ca, Zn)

sources.cite: Barge et al. 2015, From chemical gardens to chemobrionics, Chem. Rev.

silica_biogenic.name: Silica-carbonate biomorphs
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Barium/strontium carbonate co-precipitates with silica in alkaline solution, self-assembling into curved forms
examples: lab syntheses; cautionary tale for microfossil claims

sources.cite: García-Ruiz et al. 2003, Self-assembled silica-carbonate structures and detection of ancient microfossils, Science

silica_biogenic.name: Hydrothermal chimneys (Lost City carbonate; black smokers)
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Hot vent fluid mixes with cold seawater and precipitates minerals: carbonate/brucite at Lost City (40-90 °C, pH 9-11), metal sulfides at black smokers (~350 °C+)
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: black smokers can grow tens of cm/day [POP]; Lost City towers built over ~tens of kyr

sources.cite: Kelley et al. 2001, An off-axis hydrothermal vent field near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at 30°N, Nature
Kelley et al. 2005, A serpentinite-hosted ecosystem: the Lost City hydrothermal field, Science
Spiess et al. 1980, East Pacific Rise: hot springs and geophysical experiments, Science
Barge et al. 2015, From chemical gardens to chemobrionics, Chem. Rev.

silica_biogenic.name: Coral/carbonate reefs vs silica reefs
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Corals build CaCO3; siliceous sponge reefs dominated the Jurassic but declined as diatoms depleted seawater silica
colours: coral colours from living tissue; dead reef white
examples: Great Barrier Reef; Jurassic sponge reefs of Europe

sources.cite: Maldonado et al. 1999, Decline in Mesozoic reef-building sponges explained by silicon limitation, Nature

silica_biogenic.name: Phytolith-rich soils
silica_biogenic.mechanism: Plants take up dissolved silica and deposit opal bodies in cells; they persist in soil after the plant rots
silica_biogenic.growth_rate: plant-lifecycle; soil stock builds over centuries
